question: What is the difference between pass by value, reference, and pointer?

scenes.sub: Same function, three ways to hand it the data.
scenes.say: Pass by value, by reference, and by pointer. We'll write the same add one function three ways, and watch what happens to n.

scenes.head: 1 · By value: a copy
scenes.say: By value. When addOne is called, x is a brand new variable, a copy of n. Changing x to six touches only the copy. When the function returns, the copy disappears, and n is still five.

scenes.head: 2 · By reference: an alias
scenes.say: By reference. The ampersand means x is not a copy. It's another name for n itself. So x plus one changes n directly. n is now six, and nothing was copied.

scenes.head: 3 · By pointer: a copy of the address
scenes.say: By pointer. We pass the address of n. x is a copy of that address. Following it with star x reaches the real n, so n becomes six. The caller sees the ampersand, so it's obvious n might change. But x could also be null, so a careful function checks it first.

scenes.head: Side by side
scenes.say: Side by side. The call looks the same for value and reference, only the pointer needs an ampersand. What gets copied: the whole object, nothing, or just the address. Can the function change the caller's variable? Not by value, yes for the other two. Can it be null? Only a pointer. When to use: value for small types like int, const T ref for big objects you only read, and pointers when the argument is optional.

lines: By value: the function gets its own copy. Safe, but big copies are slow.
By reference: an alias, no copy. Use const T& for big read-only inputs.
By pointer: a copy of an address. Can be null, so check it.
scenes.say: By value, the function gets its own copy: safe, but copying big objects is slow. By reference, it gets an alias with no copy at all. By pointer, it gets a copy of the address, which might be null, so check it.
